problem:
An inner product on $V={R}^{3}$ is defined as $⟨x,y⟩=2{x}_{1}{y}_{1}+2{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+{x}_{3}{y}_{3}.$ 

Normalize the  vector $v=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]$ under this inner product.

examples.knowledge_point: Normalizing a Vector in an Inner Product Space
examples.problem:
Let $V=\mathcal{C}\left[0,\pi\right]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $\left[0,\pi\right],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
\langle x(t),y(t) \rangle = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi} x(t) y(t) \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

Normalize the vector $f(t)= 3t.$
examples.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is defined as

$$
\| f(t)\| = \sqrt{\langle  f(t),  f(t) \rangle}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{(3t)}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }9{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{t}^{3}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =3{\pi }^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\| f(t) \|  = \sqrt{3\pi^3} = \pi \sqrt{3\pi}.
$$

To normalize the vector $f(t),$ we divide $f(t)$ by its norm $\| f(t) \| \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\frac{f(t)}{‖f(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi \sqrt{3\pi }}\cdot 3t \\  & =\frac{t\sqrt{3}}{\pi \sqrt{\pi }}\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Let $V=C[\pi ,2\pi ]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[\pi ,2\pi ],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\,(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1)^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\,(4{cos}^{2}⁡t+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }((2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(3+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(3t+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t){|}_{\pi }^{2\pi } \\  & =(6\pi +0+0)-(3\pi +0+0) \\  & =3\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we made use of the trigonometric identity 

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡t=\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2}.
$$

Finally then,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖f(t)‖ & =\sqrt{3\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$
